entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Philoxenus of Cythera (died 379 BCE) emerged as a preeminent Greek dithyrambic poet during the late 5th and early 4th centuries BCE, a pivotal figure in the development of the "New Music" movement in Athens and beyond. His innovative approach to dithyramb, characterized by elaborate musicality, complex rhythms, and often a departure from traditional narrative structures, significantly influenced the trajectory of Greek lyrical poetry and music. Operating primarily within the vibrant cultural milieu of Dionysian festivals, Philoxenus challenged established aesthetic norms, earning both fervent admirers and staunch critics, including the comic playwrights and even Plato himself, who perceived his style as a radical break from classical restraint.

Philoxenus composed numerous dithyrambs, though only fragments and titles survive, with his most famous work being the cyclical poem *Cyclops* (also known as *Galatea*). This work reimagined the myth of Odysseus and Polyphemus, notably portraying the Cyclops as a lovelorn shepherd rather than a monstrous brute, a thematic innovation that was highly controversial. His poetry was known for its technical virtuosity, employing intricate melodic lines and instrumental accompaniment that pushed the boundaries of traditional performance, incorporating elements like extended vocalizations and virtuosic instrumental passages, particularly for the aulos.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Philoxenus of Cythera was a leading innovator of the "New Music" in ancient Greece, whose bold dithyrambic compositions challenged traditional forms and significantly influenced the trajectory of Greek lyrical poetry and music towards greater complexity and expressiveness. His work provoked critical debate and paved the way for later Hellenistic musical developments.
